title: SAT 14 · Fractions of quantities
description: A/B reasoning practice. Difficulty is editorial, not standardized SAT calibration.

questions.title: Finding the Fraction of Students Who Chose Apples
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A class survey records the favorite fruit of 20 students. According to the chart, 8 students chose apples, 6 chose bananas, 4 chose grapes, and 2 chose oranges. What fraction of the students chose apples? Choose A or B and justify your answer mathematically.
questions.explanation: The fraction is the number who chose apples divided by the total number of students: \(\frac{8}{20}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(4\) gives \(\frac{2}{5}\). Choice B, \(\frac{2}{3}\), equals \(\frac{8}{12}\): it compares the 8 apple choosers with the other 12 students (part to part) instead of with all 20 students.

visuals.alt: Bar chart of favorite fruits among 20 students: apples 8, bananas 6, grapes 4, and oranges 2.

questions.hint: Read the apples bar and the total number of students, write apples over the total, and simplify.

questions.title: Recovering a Ribbon's Whole Length
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: Three-eighths of a ribbon is 15 centimeters long. What is the ribbon's total length? Choose A or B and explain how you recover the whole from a fractional part.
questions.explanation: If \(\frac{3}{8}\) of the ribbon is 15 centimeters, then \(\frac{1}{8}\) is \(15\div3=5\) centimeters. The whole ribbon has eight eighths, so its length is \(8\times5=40\) centimeters. Choice A incorrectly multiplies 15 by 3 without accounting for all eight equal parts.
questions.hint: Find the length of one-eighth from the three-eighths, then build up to eight eighths.

questions.title: Counting the Green Counters
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A box contains 24 counters. One-quarter of the counters are red, one-third are blue, and every counter has exactly one color. The remaining counters are green. How many counters are green? Choose A or B and show the parts of the whole.
questions.explanation: One-quarter of 24 is \(24\div4=6\) red counters, and one-third of 24 is \(24\div3=8\) blue counters. Thus, \(24-6-8=10\) counters are green. Equivalently, the green fraction is \(1-\frac14-\frac13=\frac{5}{12}\), and \(\frac{5}{12}\times24=10\). Choice B leaves too few counters for the stated red and blue groups.
questions.hint: Find how many counters are red and how many are blue, then subtract both from the total.

questions.title: The Fraction Outside Both Activities
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: In a group of 30 students, \(\frac{2}{5}\) play football, \(\frac{1}{3}\) play basketball, and \(\frac{1}{6}\) play both sports. What fraction of the students play neither sport? Choose A or B and use the regions of the Venn diagram.
questions.explanation: The fraction who play at least one sport is \(\frac25+\frac13-\frac16=\frac{12}{30}+\frac{10}{30}-\frac{5}{30}=\frac{17}{30}\). The overlap is subtracted once because those students were counted in both groups. Therefore, the fraction who play neither is \(1-\frac{17}{30}=\frac{13}{30}\), matching the 13 students outside both circles. Choice A is the fraction who play at least one sport, not neither.

visuals.alt: Venn diagram for 30 students: 7 play only football, 5 only basketball, 5 play both, and 13 play neither.

questions.hint: Add the football and basketball fractions, subtract the overlap once, and take the rest of the whole; the Venn regions can confirm the count.

questions.title: Finding the Full Capacity of a Water Tank
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A water tank is \(\frac{3}{5}\) full when it contains 27 liters of water. What is the tank's full capacity? Choose A or B and show how the fraction determines the whole capacity.
questions.explanation: If \(\frac35\) of the capacity is 27 liters, then one-fifth is \(27\div3=9\) liters. Five-fifths is \(5\times9=45\) liters. Choice A is too small because three-fifths of 40 liters is only 24 liters.
questions.hint: Find the amount for one-fifth of the tank from the three-fifths, then build up to five-fifths.

questions.title: A Quarter of Each Flour Batch
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A recipe diagram maps the total flour in a batch to the amount reserved for topping. The topping always uses one-quarter of the total flour. If a batch contains 28 cups of flour in total, how many cups are reserved for topping? Choose A or B and explain the proportional rule.
questions.explanation: The mapping confirms that the topping amount is one-quarter of the total. For 28 cups, \(\frac14\times28=28\div4=7\) cups are reserved. Choice B would be correct for a total of 24 cups, not 28.

visuals.alt: Mapping diagram showing one-quarter of each total flour amount: 8 maps to 2 cups, 12 maps to 3 cups, and 20 maps to 5 cups.

questions.hint: Use the mapping pairs to confirm the one-quarter rule, then apply it to 28 cups.

questions.title: Students in the Science Club
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A school has 360 students. Five-twelfths of them join an after-school club, and two-thirds of the club members join the science club. How many students join the science club? Choose A or B and calculate the fraction of the whole school.
questions.explanation: The number in after-school clubs is \(\frac{5}{12}\times360=150\). Two-thirds of those students are in the science club, so \(\frac23\times150=100\). Equivalently, the science club contains \(\frac23\times\frac{5}{12}=\frac{5}{18}\) of the whole school, and \(\frac{5}{18}\times360=100\). Choice A is one-third of the whole school, which ignores the fact that two-thirds is taken only from the 150 students who joined an after-school club.
questions.hint: Find how many students join any after-school club first; the two-thirds applies only to that group.

questions.title: The Fraction of Reference Books
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A library has 240 books: 90 fiction books, 60 nonfiction books, and the rest reference books. The table summarizes the collection. What fraction of all the books are reference books? Choose A or B and simplify the fraction.
questions.explanation: The number of reference books is \(240-90-60=90\). The fraction is \(\frac{90}{240}\). Dividing both numbers by 30 simplifies it to \(\frac{3}{8}\). Choice B, \(\frac14\), would represent 60 of the 240 books rather than 90.

visuals.alt: Table showing 90 fiction books, 60 nonfiction books, 90 reference books, and 240 books in total.

questions.hint: Find the number of reference books from the table, write it over the total, and simplify.

questions.title: Reading a Part-Whole Function Graph
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A function graph models a part \(y\) that is three-quarters of a whole \(x\), so \(y=\frac34x\). If the whole is 28 units, what is the corresponding part? Choose A or B and explain how the graph represents the fraction.
questions.explanation: Substitute the whole, \(x=28\), into the rule: \(y=\frac34\times28=21\). The graph's point \((28,21)\) shows the same relationship. Choice A is three-quarters of 24, not three-quarters of the stated whole, 28.

visuals.alt: A straight line y=0.75x through the origin, including the point (28,21), showing that the part is three-quarters of the whole.

questions.hint: Substitute the whole into y = (3/4)x and check the point on the graph.

questions.title: Recovering a School's Total Budget
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A school spends \(\frac{2}{5}\) of its annual budget on salaries and \(\frac{1}{3}\) on facilities. The remaining budget is 16,000 dollars. What is the total annual budget? Choose A or B and explain how the remaining fraction determines the whole.
questions.explanation: The remaining fraction is \(1-\frac25-\frac13=\frac{15}{15}-\frac{6}{15}-\frac{5}{15}=\frac{4}{15}\). Thus, \(\frac{4}{15}\) of the budget equals 16,000 dollars. One-fifteenth is 4,000 dollars, so the whole budget is \(15\times4{,}000=60{,}000\) dollars. Choice B would leave only \(\frac{4}{15}\times48{,}000=12{,}800\) dollars, not 16,000.
questions.hint: Find the fraction of the budget that remains after the two expenses, then use the 16,000 dollars to find the size of one share.

questions.title: The Planted Part of a Rectangular Field
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A rectangular field is 15 meters long and 8 meters wide. Three-eighths of its area is planted with flowers. The diagram gives the field's dimensions. What area is planted with flowers? Choose A or B and show the part-whole calculation.
questions.explanation: The total area is \(15\times8=120\) square meters. Three-eighths of this area is \(\frac38\times120=3\times15=45\) square meters. Choice A is half the total field, but the planted area is only three-eighths of the field.

visuals.alt: A rectangular field ABCD, 15 meters by 8 meters. The diagram gives the whole field; the flower beds occupy three-eighths of its area as stated in the question.

questions.hint: Find the area of the whole field first, then take three-eighths of it.

questions.title: Finding the Whole Class from a Fraction of a Fraction
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: Thirty girls in a class take music lessons. This is three-quarters of all the girls, and girls make up four-sevenths of the whole class. How many students are in the class? Choose A or B and show both steps.
questions.explanation: If 30 is three-quarters of the number of girls, the number of girls is \(30\div\frac34=30\times\frac43=40\). Those 40 girls are four-sevenths of the class, so the total class size is \(40\div\frac47=40\times\frac74=70\). Choice B would make 40 girls more than four-sevenths of the class, so it does not satisfy both statements.
questions.hint: Use the 30 music students to find the number of girls, then use the number of girls to find the whole class.

questions.title: Reconstructing the Original Marble Count
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A bag of marbles has some original number of marbles. First, one-quarter of the marbles are removed. Then one-third of the marbles remaining after the first removal are removed. There are 18 marbles left. How many marbles were in the bag originally? Choose A or B and reason backward through the fractions.
questions.explanation: After the first removal, \(\frac34\) of the original amount remains. After the second removal, \(\frac23\) of that remainder stays. The final fraction is \(\frac34\times\frac23=\frac12\) of the original amount. If half is 18 marbles, the original count is \(18\times2=36\). Choice B would leave \(\frac12\times30=15\) marbles, not 18.
questions.hint: Find what fraction of the original remains after both removals by multiplying the remaining fractions.

questions.title: Counting the Orange Candies
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A jar contains 48 candies. One-third of the candies are strawberry-flavored. One-quarter of the candies left after the strawberry candies are set aside are lemon-flavored. All remaining candies are orange-flavored. How many candies are orange-flavored? Choose A or B and track each part of the whole.
questions.explanation: One-third of 48 is 16 strawberry candies, leaving \(48-16=32\). One-quarter of the remaining 32 is 8 lemon candies, leaving \(32-8=24\) orange candies. Choice A results from subtracting the lemon fraction from the original 48 rather than from the 32 candies that remain after the strawberry candies are removed.
questions.hint: Remove the strawberry candies first; the one-quarter applies only to the candies that remain.

questions.title: Finding a Tank's Capacity from the Empty Fraction
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: An empty tank is filled in two stages. First, water fills two-fifths of its total capacity. Next, water fills one-third of the space that is still empty. After these stages, 48 liters of space remain empty. What is the tank's full capacity? Choose A or B and justify the fractions used.
questions.explanation: Let \(C\) be the capacity in liters. After the first stage, \(3C/5\) is empty. The second stage fills \(\frac13\cdot\frac35 C=C/5\). The empty space left is \(3C/5-C/5=2C/5\). Since \(2C/5=48\) L, \(C/5=24\) L and \(C=120\) L. A is correct. For B, a 96-liter tank would leave \(2(96)/5=38.4\) L empty, not 48 L.
questions.hint: Represent the capacity by a variable. Apply the second fraction to the empty space remaining after the first stage.

questions.title: Reconstructing Savings After Two Expenses
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A student spends three-eighths of their savings on a trip. Later, the student spends one-fifth of the money that remains on books. After both expenses, 84 dollars remain. How much money did the student have before spending anything? Choose A or B and show how the remaining fractions combine.
questions.explanation: After the first expense, \(1-\frac38=\frac58\) of the savings remains. After spending one-fifth of that remainder, \(\frac45\) of it remains. The final amount is \(\frac58\times\frac45=\frac12\) of the original savings. If half is 84 dollars, the original amount was \(84\times2=168\) dollars. Choice A would leave 80 dollars after these two expenses, not 84.
questions.hint: Multiply the fractions that remain after each expense to find what fraction of the savings is left.

questions.title: Capacity After Losing and Adding Water
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A tank is initially three-quarters full. It loses two-fifths of the water it contains. Then 14 liters of water are added, and the tank becomes four-fifths full. What is the tank's total capacity? Choose A or B and set up an equation using fractions of the whole capacity.
questions.explanation: Let the tank's capacity be \(C\) liters. Initially it contains \(\frac34C\). Losing two-fifths of that amount leaves \(\frac35\times\frac34C=\frac9{20}C\). After adding 14 liters, the amount is \(\frac45C\), so \(\frac9{20}C+14=\frac45C\). Therefore, \(14=\left(\frac{16}{20}-\frac9{20}\right)C=\frac7{20}C\), giving \(C=14\times\frac{20}{7}=40\) liters. Choice A does not satisfy the equation: for a capacity of 35 liters, the amount after the loss and addition would be \(\frac9{20}\times35+14=29.75\) liters, whereas four-fifths of 35 liters is 28 liters.
questions.hint: Write each stage as a fraction of the capacity C, then set the final amount equal to four-fifths of C.

questions.title: Juice Capacity After a Fractional Change
questions.learningObjective: Apply fractions of quantities and justify the selected answer.
questions.question: A container is initially seven-eighths full of juice. One-third of the juice is poured out, and then 4 liters of juice are added. The container is now three-quarters full. What is the container's total capacity? Choose A or B and justify the equation using the part-whole relationship.
questions.explanation: Let the capacity be \(C\) liters. After one-third of the juice is poured out, two-thirds of the original juice remains, so the amount is \(\frac23\times\frac78C=\frac7{12}C\). Adding 4 liters makes it three-quarters full: \(\frac7{12}C+4=\frac34C\). Since \(\frac34=\frac9{12}\), we get \(4=\frac2{12}C=\frac16C\), so \(C=24\) liters. Choice B would require 5 liters to increase the amount from \(\frac7{12}\) to \(\frac34\) of the container, not 4 liters.
questions.hint: Write the amount after pouring as a fraction of the capacity C, add 4, and set it equal to three-quarters of C.
